The inter-school quiz prize was two thousand rupees, and Ujjwal had the envelope in his blazer by lunch. By the last bell, most of it was gone. He had bought cold drinks and samosas for the whole class at the canteen, a new pair of earphones, and a comic from the book fair in the school hall.
"You've spent it all?" Kishore asked, stuffing a samosa in his mouth.
"It was prize money, yaar. Free money."
"But you won't even buy a chai with your tuition money."
Ujjwal went quiet. He taught maths to two kids in his building every evening and kept that money folded in a book at home. "That's different. I earned that."
Kishore shrugged. "You earned the quiz too. You studied for weeks."

qa.q: What did Ujjwal buy for the whole class?
qa.a: He bought cold drinks and samosas for the whole class at the canteen.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal feel it was fine to spend the prize money so quickly?
qa.a: To Ujjwal the prize felt like "free money" for fun, unlike the tuition money he earned by teaching, so spending it felt guilt-free.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal try the next time he gets a windfall?
qa.a: Keep it for a few days before spending and ask whether he would spend the same amount from his tuition money; if not, he may want to slow down.

qa.q: How does Kishore see the difference Ujjwal is making?
qa.a: Kishore doesn't see much difference, since Ujjwal studied for weeks to win the quiz, so both sums were earned in their own way.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy spending a prize quickly as fun money while guarding money he earned, though each rupee is worth the same.

Dear Chinmay,
Guess what, I got my birthday money from Grandpa in Kochi: three thousand rupees! I spent it in one weekend. A football, two video games, pizza with the boys, and a hoodie I didn't really need. It felt great.
The weird thing is, I also have the money from my newspaper round. Four months of getting up at six. I haven't spent a single rupee of that. Last week I wanted new football boots and I didn't touch it. I kept thinking, that's real money.
My mum says money is money, and I know she's right. Every rupee buys the same stuff. But when it comes from a birthday card, it feels like it's for having fun, and when I earn it, it feels like it's for something serious.
Are you like this too?
Your cousin brother,
Thomas

qa.q: How much birthday money did Thomas get from Grandpa?
qa.a: Thomas got three thousand rupees from Grandpa in Kochi.

qa.q: Why does the newspaper money feel like "real money" to Thomas?
qa.a: Thomas feels proud of the newspaper money because he earned it by getting up at six for four months, so he is careful with it, while the birthday money felt meant for fun.

qa.q: What would you advise Thomas about his next birthday money?
qa.a: Before spending, imagine it came from the newspaper round and ask if the purchase still feels worth it; that helps treat every rupee the same way.

qa.q: Why might Thomas's mum react differently to his spending?
qa.a: She sees all the money as the same, so she probably wishes he had been as careful with the birthday money as he is with his earnings.

grounding: It shows a teenager who spends gift money freely as fun money while guarding his earned money, though every rupee is the same.

Thomas, you asked what happened to the scholarship money, so here goes. I'm Noor, Abbu's eldest son, and I won the district essay prize in Class 10: four thousand rupees. My Abbu said, "Your prize, your choice." I was so happy I felt like I'd found treasure. In two weeks it was all gone: new shoes, gaming credits, treating my cousins to ice cream, and a phone cover I lost in a month.
Meanwhile, I'd been helping at my uncle's shop every Saturday, and I kept that money in an envelope under my mattress. I would never touch it. That was my serious money.
Now I look back and it's funny. The prize money was just as much mine. I even worked harder for it, rewriting that essay five times. My brain just filed it under fun.

qa.q: How much was Noor's district essay prize?
qa.a: The district essay prize was four thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Noor feel free to spend the prize money so fast?
qa.a: Winning it felt like finding treasure, so Noor's mind filed it under fun, while the shop money felt like serious money to protect.

qa.q: What could Noor do differently with a future prize?
qa.a: Put it in the same envelope as the shop money first, then decide calmly what to spend, since it was just as much Noor's and worked for just as hard.

qa.q: How might Noor's Abbu see how the prize money was spent?
qa.a: He gave Noor the choice, so he may accept it, though he might also wish some had lasted longer than a lost phone cover.

grounding: It shows a teenager who spent prize money quickly as fun money while guarding earned money, though all of it was equally the teenager's.

passage: I'm Suraj, Wasim's neighbour in the chawl. Wasim gets up at five every day to deliver newspapers, and he keeps that money in a steel box under his bed. He won't even buy a vada pav from it. "That's for my phone," he says. Last Sunday he won player of the match at the inter-colony cricket final: a thousand rupees in an envelope. By evening he had treated eight of us to falooda, bought new batting gloves and a cap he didn't need, and topped up his game credits. When I asked why he didn't put it in the steel box, he looked at me like I was mad. "Prize money is for enjoying, yaar." I don't know exactly what goes on in his head. But a rupee is a rupee, isn't it?

qa.q: Where does Wasim keep his newspaper money?
qa.a: In a steel box under his bed.

qa.q: Why does Wasim feel prize money is for enjoying while newspaper money isn't?
qa.a: The newspaper money comes from waking at five every day, so it feels earned and serious, while the prize arrived all at once and felt like a bonus for fun.

qa.q: What could Wasim do the next time he wins prize money?
qa.a: He could put part of it in the steel box before celebrating, so the prize also helps the phone he works so hard for.

qa.q: How might Suraj and the other friends see Wasim's falooda treat?
qa.a: They probably enjoyed it and saw Wasim as big-hearted, though Suraj also wonders why a prize rupee feels different to Wasim from an earned one 🤔

grounding: A neighbour watches a teenage boy guard his earned money but spend a prize in a day, as if the rupees were different.

Eid, Monday: Ayesha Khala pressed two thousand rupees into Irshad's hand. "Eidi, for you." By Wednesday he had spent most of it: a gaming headset, burgers for his cricket team and a pair of sunglasses. It felt light and easy, like money from nowhere.
The next Saturday: Irshad did his usual shift at his uncle's grocery, stacking rice bags, and was paid three hundred. His classmate Kavitha asked to borrow fifty for a notebook. "No way," he said. "I sweated for that."
Two weeks later: The school trip form came: eight hundred rupees. Irshad counted what was left: the three hundred in wages and forty rupees of Eidi. He stared at the sunglasses on his desk. "It was all the same money," he said out loud to the empty room.

qa.q: What did Irshad buy with the Eidi?
qa.a: A gaming headset, burgers for his cricket team and a pair of sunglasses.

qa.q: How did Irshad feel about his wages compared with the Eidi?
qa.a: Irshad felt protective of the wages he had sweated for and refused to lend any, while the Eidi felt light and easy, so he spent it in days.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Irshad, and what could he do differently next time?
qa.a: Counting his money for the trip form showed him that all rupees are the same; next time he could set aside part of any gift before spending.

qa.q: How might Kavitha have felt when Irshad refused fifty rupees?
qa.a: Kavitha may have felt hurt or surprised, having seen Irshad spend freely on burgers and sunglasses only days before.

grounding: A teenage boy spends gift money quickly while guarding his wages, until a trip form shows him every rupee counts the same.

Saturday
Won the district essay competition!! 3,000 rupees prize. It felt like free money, so today I took Shalini and the gang for pizza, bought those shoes, and now there's about 200 left.
Here's the weird part. I also have 2,500 from tutoring the neighbours' kids all summer. That money is sitting in my drawer, untouched, and I would NEVER spend it on pizza. I earned it. Every rupee has a Class 5 fraction problem attached.
Shalini asked why I'm so careful with one and so careless with the other. I didn't have an answer. A rupee is a rupee. My brain just sorts them into different boxes: 'fun' and 'real'.
I'm not sorry about the pizza. But next time I win something, maybe I'll wait a week and decide with Papa before it all goes.
Jatin

qa.a: Shalini sees the same rupees treated completely differently: careful with one pile, careless with the other.

passage: When Arnab won the school quiz in Krishnanagar, the headmaster handed him an envelope with a thousand rupees in front of everyone. By the next evening it was nearly gone: a cricket bat from the Sunday haat, rosogollas for the whole lane, a cheap watch that stopped by Tuesday. His mother, Leela, watched without a word. Then on Wednesday, when she asked him to lend fifty rupees for the gas cylinder till payday, Arnab hesitated. "That's my fish-market money, Ma. From helping Baba at five every morning." "And the quiz money?" "That was... prize money." Leela smiled a little. "Both are yours. Both are rupees. One you earned with your head, one with your early mornings." Arnab thought about the stopped watch. He gave her the fifty, and for once it didn't feel like a loss.

qa.q: Where did Arnab buy the cricket bat?
qa.a: At the Sunday haat.

qa.q: Why did Arnab hesitate to lend the fish-market money?
qa.a: Arnab felt protective of it because it was earned with early mornings, while the prize money had felt like fun money to spend.

qa.q: What did Leela's words help Arnab see?
qa.a: That both piles are his and both are rupees, so he could weigh a real need like the gas cylinder without sorting money by where it came from.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt watching the quiz money disappear?
qa.a: Leela seems to have felt quietly amused and patient, waiting for the right moment to talk.

grounding: Shows a teenager spending prize money freely while guarding money he earned, until his mother points out both are the same rupees.

Gabriel won the school poetry prize in Montreal: a cheque and a certificate. He cashed it on Friday and by Monday had spent it all on a new video game, pizza for his friends, and a hoodie he'd barely looked at before.

His friend Nour watched him buy the hoodie. "Didn't you say you were saving for a bike?"

"That's my job money," Gabriel said. He worked Saturdays at a bakery. "This is prize money. It's like it fell from the sky."

A week later the bike he wanted went on sale. Gabriel checked his job savings and winced. Still not enough.

"The prize would have covered it," Nour said.

Gabriel stared at the hoodie on his chair. It suddenly felt much less fun.

qa.q: Where did Gabriel work on Saturdays?
qa.a: He worked Saturdays at a bakery.

qa.q: Why did spending the prize money quickly feel fine to Gabriel?
qa.a: He felt happy and carefree about it, as if it fell from the sky, while his bakery money felt hard-earned.

qa.q: What could Gabriel try the next time he wins money?
qa.a: He could pause and think about the bike or other goals, perhaps talking with a parent before deciding how to use it.

qa.q: How might Nour feel watching Gabriel buy the hoodie?
qa.a: Nour seems a little concerned and puzzled, since Gabriel had said he was saving for a bike.

grounding: A teenager spends prize money quickly as fun money while guarding money he earned.

In the college canteen, Sachin had just got a cash award for topping the district science quiz. His friend Amandeep grinned. "Treat!"

Sachin ordered samosas and cold drinks for the whole table, then bought a new pair of earphones at the stall near the gate. "Easy come, easy go," he laughed.

That evening, his tuition teacher asked everyone to buy a new reference book. Sachin had money saved from tutoring younger kids. He hesitated.

"Just use your tutoring money," Amandeep said.

"No way. I worked for that."

"You didn't work for the quiz?"

Sachin paused. He had studied for weeks for the quiz. He felt a bit sheepish and stayed quiet.

Dear Ira,

You asked what I did with the money from the essay prize. Honestly, it's gone. I bought a speaker, a bunch of snacks for the hostel, and a jacket I've worn twice. It felt like bonus money, so I didn't think.

Funny thing is, the money I earn from weekend tutoring sits untouched. When my phone screen cracked last month, I didn't want to use it. I walked around with a cracked screen for weeks instead.

It's the same money. A rupee is a rupee. But one felt like a gift and the other felt like me.

I think next time I'll talk to Papa before spending a prize.

Write soon,
Pranav

Bhavna, you asked for a money story for the podcast. I'm Vishal, Class 11.
Last year I won five thousand rupees at the inter-school quiz. Prize money! It felt like it fell from the sky, so I treated it like sky money. Pizza for the team, new earphones, a jersey, movie tickets. Gone in eight days.
Now here's the funny part. That same month I earned two thousand rupees tutoring my neighbour's son in maths, every evening for four weeks. That money I guarded like a dragon. I wouldn't even buy a samosa with it.
Same rupees. Honestly the same. But one felt like it didn't count, and the other felt like my own sweat.
My mother pointed out that if I'd treated the prize like the tutoring money, I'd have the bicycle I kept wanting. Now I tell myself: a rupee from the sky is still a rupee.

qa.q: How much did Vishal win at the quiz?
qa.a: Vishal won five thousand rupees at the inter-school quiz.

qa.q: Why did Vishal spend the prize money so fast?
qa.a: Vishal felt excited, as if the prize had fallen from the sky, so spending it seemed like fun, unlike the tutoring money that felt earned.

qa.q: What does Vishal now say to remember, and why does it help?
qa.a: 'A rupee from the sky is still a rupee', which reminds Vishal to treat all money the same whatever its source.

qa.q: How might Vishal's mother have felt about the eight days?
qa.a: His mother may have felt a little frustrated but patient, pointing to the bicycle rather than scolding.

grounding: Shows a teenager who spent prize money as fun money while guarding earned tutoring money, though every rupee was the same.

March. Pema's aunt sent three thousand rupees for Pema's sixteenth birthday. That weekend it all went: a gaming headset, a hoodie, and treats for Tushar and the others. "Birthday money is for fun," Pema said.
April. Pema started weekend shifts at the cafe near the bus stand, washing cups for three hundred rupees a day. By the end of the month there were two thousand four hundred rupees in the tin, and Pema wouldn't touch a coin. When Tushar suggested splitting a pizza, Pema refused. "That's work money."
May. Pema's phone screen cracked. The repair cost two thousand. Pema stared at the tin. "If I'd kept even half the birthday money..."
Tushar shrugged. "Money's money. The headset doesn't know where it came from."
Pema paid for the screen from the tin, wincing, and stuck a note on it: all money counts.

qa.q: How much did Pema earn per day at the cafe?
qa.a: Pema earned three hundred rupees a day washing cups.

qa.q: Why did Pema refuse to split a pizza in April?
qa.a: Pema felt protective of the work money, which felt hard-earned, while the birthday money had felt free to spend.

qa.q: What does Pema's note, 'all money counts', suggest for next time?
qa.a: Treating a gift like earned money, so a surprise cost like a cracked screen can be met from either.

qa.q: How does Tushar see Pema's two kinds of money?
qa.a: Tushar sees them as the same, saying money is money and the headset doesn't know where it came from.

grounding: Shows a teenager who spends gift money quickly as fun money while guarding earned money, though every rupee is the same.

Tejas, you got a thousand rupees for topping the district test and spent it in two days? Ha. Let me tell you about your Gurpreet Chacha at fifteen.
I won a thousand-rupee prize for the best poem in the whole school. A thousand! In those days it was a fortune. I felt like a king, and kings spend. Sweets for my class, a cricket bat, a watch that stopped in a week. By Sunday I had nothing.
But the money I earned helping my father at the dhaba on weekends, a few rupees each time, I kept in a tin under my bed and counted every night. I wouldn't spend it on anything.
My father watched all this. One evening he poured the tin onto the bed next to the empty prize envelope and said, "Which of these rupees could pay your school fees next term?" I said, "Both." He said, "Then why did you treat one like dust?"
I've never forgotten that.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet win the prize for?
qa.a: Gurpreet won it for the best poem in the whole school.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet spend the prize money so quickly?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt proud and excited, like a king with the prize, so it seemed like fun money to spend, while the dhaba earnings felt precious.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed Gurpreet's view, and why?
qa.a: The father pouring out the tin beside the empty envelope and asking which rupees could pay school fees, showing both were the same.

qa.q: How might the father have felt watching Gurpreet that week?
qa.a: The father was probably amused but concerned, waiting for the right moment to make the point gently.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a teenage habit of spending prize money freely while guarding earned money, though every rupee was the same.

"But you just spent two thousand in forty minutes."
"That was prize money," he said, as if that explained everything. The broken drone rattled in his lap.
